theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A paint factory in Spanish Town lists 'washing out mixing tanks' as one of its activities. Waste water with paint in it runs from this work to a drain. In environmental risk terms, what is this waste water discharge?
options: An environmental aspect of the activity
A control measure that the firm has put in place
An environmental objective of the firm
A legal requirement placed on the firm

questions.stem: A manager is sorting a list into aspects and impacts. Which item is an environmental impact rather than an aspect?
options: Fuel stored in a tank beside the gully
Generator exhaust that is released every day
Fish dying in a river below the outfall
Packaging thrown into the general skip

questions.stem: A resort in Negril rates the risk of its sewage plant overflowing as likelihood 3 and consequence 5, on 1 to 5 scales. Using likelihood × consequence, what is the risk score?
A hotel in Montego Bay has rated four environmental risks on 1 to 5 scales. Using likelihood × consequence, which should the manager treat first?
options: Litter left by guests on the beach: likelihood 4, consequence 2
Noise from the bar at night: likelihood 4, consequence 3
Paper waste in the offices: likelihood 5, consequence 1
Diesel tank leaking into the sea: likelihood 3, consequence 5

questions.stem: A poultry processor in May Pen plans to expand its plant, which will increase the waste water it produces. What should the manager check first?
options: Whether neighbours have complained about the plant before
Whether its insurer will raise the premium next year
Whether it needs a new or changed environmental permit
Whether competitors have recently expanded their plants

questions.stem: Why should a manager keep a register of the environmental laws, permits and permit conditions that apply to the business?
options: So duties and conditions are known, met and checked
So staff need not follow any other rules at work
So the firm can avoid inspections by the authorities
So it can be shown to customers as advertising

questions.stem: A factory's permit says it must test its effluent every month and keep the results. The May test was missed. What should the manager do?
options: Copy April's result into the May record to keep the file complete
Wait for the next inspection and explain the gap then if anyone asks
Stop all production until the authority renews the permit
Test as soon as possible, record the gap and report it as required

questions.stem: A Kingston print shop uses a solvent cleaner that gives off harmful vapour and creates hazardous waste. Which control is highest in the hierarchy of control?
options: Give staff better masks when they use the cleaner
Change to a water-based cleaner that does the job
Store the waste solvent in a locked cage outside
Train staff to use smaller amounts of the cleaner

questions.stem: Using the waste hierarchy, which is the best option for the cardboard boxes a supermarket in Mandeville receives every day?
options: Bale the cardboard and send it for recycling
Ask suppliers to deliver in reusable crates
Burn the cardboard in a drum behind the store
Send the cardboard to the landfill each week

questions.stem: Which waste from an office building must be kept apart from general waste and handed to a licensed handler?
options: Office paper, cardboard and empty water bottles
Food scraps from the staff canteen
Grass cuttings from the grounds
Used fluorescent tubes and old batteries

questions.stem: A drum of used engine oil splits in the yard of a bus depot during heavy rain, and the oil runs toward a storm drain. What should the supervisor do first?
options: Block the drain and contain the oil with the spill kit
Hose the oil away so the yard is safe to walk on
Write an incident report before anyone touches the spill
Call the supplier to ask for a replacement drum

questions.stem: Why should a firm test its environmental emergency plan with drills?
options: To show staff that the plan will probably never be needed at all
To replace the need for spill kits and other equipment
To check staff know their roles and to find gaps in the plan
To meet a rule that drills must be held every single week

questions.stem: A food warehouse in Portmore stands on low ground beside a gully. Which environmental risk most needs a plan before the hurricane season?
options: Higher electricity bills in the summer months
Dust from the car park blowing about in the dry weather
Delivery trucks arriving late in heavy traffic
Flood water carrying stored chemicals into the gully

questions.stem: A quarry manager in St Catherine wants to reduce dust complaints from a nearby community. What is the best first step?
options: Put up a sign saying the quarry meets all the rules
Meet residents to learn when and where dust is worst
Ask staff not to talk to residents about the dust
Wait for the complaints to stop once the rainy season comes

questions.stem: What should a firm's environmental policy, signed by the managing director, include?
options: A list of every staff member's job description
The prices the firm charges for each of its main products in Jamaica
A commitment to meet the law, prevent pollution and improve
The names of the firm's main competitors in Jamaica

questions.stem: An environmental management system often follows the plan-do-check-act cycle. Which activity belongs to the 'check' stage?
options: Measuring results and auditing against the plan
Setting the objectives and targets for the coming year
Training staff and putting controls in place
Changing the plan after the review meeting

questions.stem: A hotel wants a fair measure of its water use that allows for busy and quiet months. Which indicator is best?
options: Litres used per occupied room night
Total litres used in the whole year
Number of taps fitted in the hotel
Cost of the water bill each month

questions.stem: After leaks were repaired, a factory's water use fell from 2,500 m³ a month to 2,000 m³ a month. What is the percentage reduction?
In one month a resort in Ocho Rios produced 40 tonnes of waste and recycled or composted 12 tonnes of it. What percentage was kept out of landfill?
Solar panels for an office in Mandeville cost J$6,000,000 and will cut the electricity bill by J$1,500,000 a year. What is the simple payback period?
options: 2.5 years
4 years
6 years
9 years

questions.stem: A cleaner at a Kingston office tells her supervisor that she poured leftover bleach down the storm drain outside. What should the supervisor do?
options: Tell her not to mention it to anyone else in the office
Give her a written warning before finding out what happened
Record and report the incident, and arrange retraining
Ignore it, as a small amount of bleach does no harm

questions.stem: Why should a manager encourage staff to report environmental near misses, such as a drum that almost fell off a forklift?
options: So that staff who report them can be disciplined
So causes are fixed before real harm is done
So the firm shows fewer incidents on its record
So the insurer can refuse to pay future claims

questions.stem: A hotel hires a contractor to empty its kitchen grease traps. What should the hotel check before the work starts?
options: That the contractor is licensed and disposes of waste lawfully
That the contractor is the cheapest firm in the parish
That the contractor works only at night while the guests are asleep
That the contractor uses the hotel's own truck for the job

questions.stem: Which purchasing choice best reduces an office's environmental risk from cleaning products?
options: Buying the products in the smallest bottles on sale
Choosing the supplier whose packaging looks brightest on the shelf
Ordering extra stock so the office never runs out
Choosing low-toxicity products that have a safety data sheet

questions.stem: New staff at a bottling plant in Spanish Town will handle caustic cleaning chemicals. When should they be trained in spill response?
options: After their first year, at the annual training day
Only if a spill happens during one of their shifts
When the plant is next inspected by the authority
Before they start handling the chemicals

questions.stem: A hotel's standby diesel generator runs for long hours during power cuts. Which environmental risks should the manager control?
options: Fumes, noise and fuel leaks affecting guests and neighbours
Too much shade falling on the hotel's swimming pool in the afternoon
Guests disliking the colour of the generator housing
Staff taking too long over their lunch breaks

questions.stem: Old air-conditioning units at a call centre in Montego Bay are being replaced. What should happen to the refrigerant gas inside them?
options: Release it outdoors, where it will spread out safely
Have a trained technician recover it for proper handling
Leave it in the units and send them to the dump
Sell the units with the gas still in them for scrap

questions.stem: Which group is an external stakeholder in a factory's environmental performance?
options: The factory's own production supervisors
The factory's maintenance team
Residents living downstream of the factory
The factory's payroll clerk

questions.stem: A manager has added controls to a fuel store. What is meant by the 'residual risk'?
options: The risk before any controls were put in place
The risk that is left after the controls
The cost of putting the controls in place
The part of the risk passed to an insurer

questions.stem: A tour company decides to stop running a boat trip that has been damaging a coral reef. Which response to risk is this?
options: Treating the risk
Transferring the risk
Terminating the risk
Tolerating the risk

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of an internal environmental audit?
options: To find staff who should be dismissed for poor performance
To plan the firm's yearly advertising
To set the prices of the firm's products
To check whether controls and duties are being met

questions.stem: Why should a manager keep records of waste collections, such as signed waste transfer notes?
options: To show where waste went and that it was handled lawfully
To work out how much the office cleaners should be paid each month
To decide which staff should get a bonus this year
To keep a list of the firm's best customers

questions.stem: How can a manager best keep up with changes in environmental law and permit rules?
options: Watch official notices and updates, and seek advice when needed
Wait for an inspector to point out any changes
Rely on what staff remember from earlier training
Assume the rules have not changed since the permit was issued

questions.stem: A resident phones a factory in Spanish Town to complain about a strong smell. What should the manager do first?
options: Tell the resident the smell comes from another factory
Record the details, investigate and reply to the resident
Promise to close the factory until the smell stops
Ask the resident to put the complaint in a letter

questions.stem: A manager wants funds to fit a better oil interceptor at a vehicle depot. Which argument is strongest for the board?
options: The old interceptor is an ugly colour
Other depots have newer equipment
Staff would enjoy working with new, modern equipment at the depot
It cuts the risk of pollution, fines and clean-up costs

questions.stem: A bar in Negril plays loud music late at night and neighbours have complained. Which control should the manager try first?
options: Move the speakers closer to the boundary wall
Tell neighbours that the bar holds all its licences
Set sound limits and point speakers away from homes
Play the music louder earlier in the evening

questions.stem: Which is the best way to decide how often each environmental control is checked?
options: Check every control once a year, whatever the risk
Check only the controls that staff complain about
Check more often where the risk score is higher
Check only when an inspector is due to visit

questions.stem: Who is accountable for making sure a firm manages its environmental risks?
options: Only the cleaners who handle the waste
Only the outside consultant who wrote the environmental plan
Each customer who buys the firm's products
Senior management, with duties shared down the line

questions.stem: Which is NOT a good way to reduce energy use in an office?
options: Fit motion sensors to switch off lights in empty rooms
Leave computers on overnight so they start up faster
Set air conditioners to a sensible temperature
Service the air-conditioning units on schedule

questions.stem: Why should a fuel or chemical tank stand inside a bund, a sealed wall or tray around it?
options: To hold any leak so it cannot reach soil or drains
To stop staff from reading the label on the tank
To keep the tank cool in hot weather
To make the tank easier to fill from a truck

questions.stem: A beach resort plans to clear the seagrass in front of the hotel to please guests. What should the manager do?
options: Clear it at night so that guests do not see the work
Clear only a small strip without asking anyone
Ask guests to do the clearing as a fun activity
Check permits first and get expert advice on the effects

questions.stem: Which is the best environmental target for a hotel?
options: Be greener this year across the whole hotel
Use less electricity whenever possible
Cut electricity per room night by 10% by December
Ask guests to think more about the environment

questions.stem: How should a manager make sure night-shift staff know the new spill procedure?
options: Brief them in person, give a copy and check they understand
Email it to the day supervisor and hope it is passed on
Pin it on the noticeboard in the manager's private office
Mention it briefly at the end-of-year staff party

questions.stem: A fuel spill at a depot has been cleaned up. What should the manager do next?
options: Close the file at once, as the spill is gone
Find the root cause and update the controls
Blame the driver in a notice to all staff
Buy a bigger tank so spills are less likely

questions.stem: A site beside a river is described as 'high environmental risk'. Which two factors together set the level of a risk?
options: Likelihood and consequence
Cost and profit
Size and colour
Age and location

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What word names the part of an activity, product or service that can interact with the environment, such as a discharge or an emission?
What three-letter abbreviation names the structured system an organisation uses to manage its environmental duties, risks and improvement?
On scales of 1 to 5, a chemical store's spill risk is rated 4 for likelihood and 4 for consequence. Multiplying the two, what score does it get?
What document from the maker or supplier gives a chemical's hazards, safe storage and spill advice?
The improvement cycle used in many management systems is written PDCA. What do the four letters stand for?
Before a large new development near a wetland is approved, the authority may ask for a study of its likely effects. Give the three-letter abbreviation for this study.
A delivery firm's fuel use fell from 8,000 litres to 6,800 litres a month. What is the percentage reduction?
What term is used for an event that could have caused environmental harm but did not, such as a chemical drum that nearly toppled?
Solar water heaters for a guest house cost J$2,700,000 and save J$600,000 a year. What is the simple payback period in years?
What word names the written permission, with conditions, that a firm needs from the authority to discharge effluent or carry out another regulated activity?
In the waste hierarchy, what option sits at the top, above reuse, recycling and disposal?
What word describes the treated or untreated waste water discharged from a factory or sewage plant?
A hotel used 210,000 kWh of electricity in a month with 7,000 occupied room nights. How many kWh did it use per occupied room night?
What name is given to the set of absorbent pads, booms and bags kept near oil and chemical stores for cleaning up leaks?
Complete the name of the principle that the organisation causing pollution should bear the cost of putting it right: the '____ pays' principle.

essays.stem: You manage a 120-room hotel on the north coast. Plan how you would identify the hotel's environmental aspects and impacts and assess the risks, so that you can decide where to act first.
essays.modelAnswer: I would form a small team from housekeeping, kitchen, maintenance, grounds and the front office, because each knows its own work. We would walk through every area and list each activity, such as laundry, cooking, pool cleaning, generator use and waste collection, including normal running, start-up and emergencies like hurricanes. For each activity we would list the aspects, for example waste water, fuel storage, chemical use, noise and solid waste, and the impacts they could cause, such as polluted sea water, damaged reef or complaints from neighbours. I would check the permits and laws that apply, because a legal duty raises the priority. Each risk would be rated for likelihood and consequence on a 1 to 5 scale and multiplied to give a score, so that a diesel tank near the sea scoring 15 comes before office paper scoring 5. I would also ask staff and neighbours about past problems. The results go into a risk register with an owner for each risk, and I would act first on the high scores and any legal gaps.
markingPoints: Involves staff from each area and covers normal, abnormal and emergency conditions
Lists activities, then aspects, then impacts with relevant hotel examples
Checks legal and permit duties as part of the assessment
Rates likelihood and consequence and ranks the risks correctly
Records the results in a register with owners and acts on the highest risks first

essays.stem: Explain how a manager makes sure that a manufacturing business meets its environmental permits and the law, and keeps on meeting them.
essays.modelAnswer: First the manager finds out which laws and permits apply: the environment and planning authority's permits for discharges, emissions and any new building, waste rules, and the occupational safety and health law where chemicals also affect workers. She lists each duty and permit condition in a legal register, with the date it applies, who owns it and how it will be met, for example monthly effluent tests or quarterly reports. Controls and procedures are written to meet each condition, staff are trained, and equipment such as interceptors and bunds is maintained. Monitoring results are recorded and compared with the permit limits, and any breach is reported to the authority as the permit requires, with action to put it right. The register is reviewed regularly and whenever the law, the permit or the process changes, such as before an expansion. Internal audits check that the duties are really being met, and the results go to senior management. Keeping good records shows the firm has acted with care if an inspector or the public asks.
markingPoints: Identifies the laws and permits that apply, in general terms
Keeps a legal register with owners, dates and conditions
Puts controls, training and monitoring in place to meet each condition
Reports breaches as required and corrects them
Reviews the register when things change and audits compliance, keeping records

essays.stem: A food factory in St Catherine pays J$2,000,000 a year to truck away waste water that its treatment plant cannot handle, and there have been two overflows. Option A: upgrade the treatment plant for J$8,000,000, ending the trucking. Option B: build a larger holding tank for J$2,500,000 and keep trucking. Compare the options over five years and recommend one.
essays.modelAnswer: Over five years Option A costs J$8,000,000 once, because the trucking stops. Its payback is J$8,000,000 ÷ J$2,000,000 = 4 years, so after the fourth year it saves money. Option B costs J$2,500,000 plus five years of trucking at J$2,000,000, which is J$10,000,000, so J$12,500,000 in total. Option A is therefore J$4,500,000 cheaper over five years. The environmental risk also differs. Option A treats the water on site, so the overflow risk falls and the firm no longer depends on trucks arriving on time, which matters in heavy rain. Option B only stores the problem: if trucks are late during a storm the tank may still overflow, and moving waste by road brings its own spill risk. Option A needs more cash now, may need a permit change and must be run well, so staff training and maintenance must be budgeted. I recommend Option A, because it costs less over five years and lowers the main risk, with a check on permits before work starts.
markingPoints: Calculates Option A at J$8,000,000 with a 4-year payback
Calculates Option B at J$12,500,000 and the J$4,500,000 difference
Compares the environmental risk of each, not only the cost
Notes conditions such as cash, permits, training or maintenance
Makes a clear, justified recommendation

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of an environmental emergency plan for a fuel and chemical store at a bus depot, and explain why each matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The plan should start with the likely emergencies, such as a tank leak, a split drum, a fire or flooding during a hurricane, so that the response fits the real risks. It should name who is in charge on each shift and give each person a role, because confusion wastes the first minutes. It sets out the first steps: make the area safe, stop the source if this is safe, block drains and contain the spill using the spill kit, and keep people away. It lists the equipment and where it is kept, such as spill kits, drain covers, fire extinguishers and PPE, with checks to make sure it is stocked. It gives contact numbers for the fire service, the authority and a licensed waste contractor, and states who must be told and when, because some incidents must be reported. It covers clean-up and safe disposal of contaminated material. Finally, it requires training, drills and a review after every incident or drill, so that the plan keeps working.
markingPoints: Identifies the likely emergencies for the site
Gives roles and the first response steps, including containing drains
Lists equipment, its location and checks
Includes contacts, reporting duties and safe disposal
Requires training, drills and review

essays.stem: Residents near a quarry in St Catherine complain about dust and blasting noise. As the quarry manager, plan how you would work with the community and other stakeholders to manage these risks.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listening. I would meet residents and community leaders, such as the citizens' association and the church, to learn when and where the dust and noise are worst and how they affect people, for example on schoolchildren or on washing left outside. I would also involve the councillor and inform the authority, since the quarry's permits set conditions. Next I would check our own monitoring and the permit limits, and add dust and noise readings at the boundary if they are missing. I would agree practical actions, such as watering haul roads, covering trucks, slowing speeds, fixing blasting times and giving notice before each blast. I would name one contact person and set up a simple complaints log with a promised reply time. I would report back to the community every month on what we have done and the readings, including where we fell short. Working this way builds trust, reduces conflict and shows the authority that we take our duties seriously.
markingPoints: Listens to residents and identifies the main stakeholders
Checks permit conditions and monitoring data
Agrees practical controls for dust and noise
Sets up a contact person and a complaints process with reply times
Reports back regularly and explains how this builds trust

essays.stem: Recommend the key performance indicators a hotel group should use to monitor its environmental performance, and explain how the results should be reported to senior managers.
essays.modelAnswer: I would recommend a small set of indicators linked to the main risks. Energy per occupied room night and water per occupied room night are fair because they allow for busy and quiet seasons. The percentage of waste kept out of landfill shows how well recycling and composting work. The number of spills, near misses and permit breaches shows control of the serious risks, and effluent test results against permit limits show legal compliance. The number of community complaints and the time taken to answer them shows how neighbours see us. Each indicator needs a baseline, a target and an owner. Results should be collected the same way each month, checked for errors and shown on a one-page dashboard with trend charts and red, amber and green ratings. The report to senior managers should explain the causes of any change, the actions taken and any decisions or funds needed. Breaches and serious incidents should be reported at once, not left for the monthly report.
markingPoints: Recommends relevant indicators, including ones adjusted for occupancy
Includes compliance and incident indicators as well as resource use
Gives each indicator a baseline, target and owner
Describes clear reporting with trends, causes and decisions needed
Says serious breaches are reported at once

essays.stem: Explain how a manager of a coastal business should prepare for the environmental risks that a hurricane brings, before, during and after the storm.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the season, the manager should review the risk register for storm-related risks, such as flooding of chemical stores, fuel spills, sewage overflows, and debris and waste blown into the sea. Chemicals and fuel should be stored high, closed and secured, with tanks bunded and topped up only to safe levels. Drains should be cleared and loose waste and materials removed or tied down. Spill kits and generators should be checked, and staff should know their roles in the emergency plan. When a storm is announced, the team should follow a checklist: secure stores, shut valves, move chemicals away from flood areas and protect records. During the storm, people's safety comes first, and no one should go out to deal with a spill. After the storm, the team should inspect the site for leaks and damage, contain any spill, separate hazardous debris for proper disposal, and report incidents as required. Finally the manager should review what happened and update the plan.
markingPoints: Identifies storm-related environmental risks
Describes preparation of stores, fuel, drains and equipment
Uses a checklist when a storm is announced
Puts people's safety first during the storm
Inspects, cleans up, reports and reviews after the storm

essays.stem: Evaluate how a manager can control the environmental risks created by contractors and suppliers, such as waste haulers and cleaning firms.
essays.modelAnswer: A firm remains responsible for its waste and its site even when others do the work, so contractor control matters. Before hiring, the manager should check that waste haulers and other contractors hold the licences and permits the work needs, ask how and where they dispose of waste, and look at their record. The environmental requirements should be written into the contract, such as safe handling, spill response and the records to be returned. Contractors should be inducted on site rules, spill kits and emergency contacts before they start. During the work, supervisors should check that rules are followed, and waste transfer notes should be kept and matched to collections. For suppliers, the firm can choose less harmful products, ask for safety data sheets and less packaging, and take back empty containers. These controls work well when they are checked; a signed contract alone is weak if no one inspects. The best approach combines careful selection, clear contract terms, induction, monitoring and regular review of each contractor's performance.
markingPoints: Explains that the firm stays responsible for work done for it
Checks licences, disposal routes and record before hiring
Writes environmental requirements into contracts and inducts contractors
Monitors work and keeps waste records; uses purchasing to cut risk
Evaluates which controls work best and why checking matters

essays.stem: Staff at a manufacturing plant often ignore the waste separation and spill rules. Plan how you would build their understanding and commitment.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first find out why the rules are ignored by talking to staff and supervisors. The reasons may be lack of training, bins in the wrong place, too little time, or a belief that the rules do not matter. I would then explain the purpose clearly, using local examples such as a fish kill in a nearby river, the cost of fines and clean-up, and the effect on the plant's licence and jobs. Training would be short, practical and given on each shift, with a demonstration of the spill kit, and I would check understanding with a quick exercise. I would make the right behaviour easy: colour-coded bins where waste is made, clear signs and stocked spill kits. Supervisors would lead by example and correct problems on the spot. I would involve staff by forming a small green team to suggest improvements, and recognise good work. Finally I would track results, such as contamination in recycling bins and near-miss reports, and share progress at team meetings.
markingPoints: Finds the reasons the rules are ignored
Explains the purpose with relevant examples and consequences
Provides practical training on every shift and checks understanding
Makes compliance easy and has supervisors lead by example
Involves staff, recognises good work and tracks results

essays.stem: A diesel spill at a depot reached a gully before it was contained. Describe how you would investigate the incident and use the findings to improve the management of environmental risks.
essays.modelAnswer: Once the spill was contained and reported as required, I would set up a small investigation team, including a supervisor from another area to keep it fair. We would secure evidence: photographs, maintenance and fuel records, the spill kit check sheet and statements from the people involved, taken in a calm, no-blame way. We would set out what happened step by step and ask 'why' until we reached the root causes, for example a corroded hose that was not on the inspection list, a drain without a cover, and staff who did not know where the spill kit was. For each cause we would agree a corrective action with an owner and a date, such as adding hoses to the checklist, fitting drain covers and running a drill. I would update the risk register, since the likelihood was higher than we thought, and revise the emergency plan. The findings would be shared with staff and reported to senior management. Later, an audit would check that the actions were done and are working.
markingPoints: Contains and reports the incident, then sets up a fair investigation
Collects evidence and finds root causes, not just blame
Agrees corrective actions with owners and dates
Updates the risk register and the emergency plan
Shares lessons and checks later that actions worked

practical1.title: Environmental risk assessment and register for a business site
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case pack for a business site, such as a small hotel, a bakery or a vehicle depot in Jamaica. It includes a site plan, a list of activities, chemical and fuel stores, waste and water records, the site's permit conditions and two complaint letters from neighbours. As a group, prepare an environmental risk assessment and an action plan for the manager. Each member has a named role: aspects lead (lists each activity with its aspects and impacts in a table); legal register officer (lists the permit conditions and other legal duties in general terms, with who owns each); risk analyst (rates likelihood and consequence for each risk and builds the risk register and matrix in a spreadsheet, checking every score twice); controls planner (proposes controls for the top five risks using the hierarchy of control, with an owner, cost estimate in J$ and date); and the communications lead (drafts a reply to one neighbour and a one-page briefing for the manager). In a group of four, the aspects lead also drafts the reply to the neighbour. The group presents its top risks and action plan to the assessor for 10 minutes, and each member presents their own part.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: site plan, activity list, records, permit conditions and complaint letters
Computers with word processing and spreadsheet software
Aspects and impacts table, risk register and action plan templates
Flipchart paper, markers and coloured stickers for the site plan
photos: The site plan marked with the main aspects and risk areas
The risk register and matrix on screen, with scores
The action plan for the top five risks and the reply to the neighbour
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Aspects and impacts are correctly told apart and cover normal and emergency conditions
Legal and permit duties are listed in general terms with owners, without quoting sections
Risk scores are calculated correctly and ranked, and were checked twice
Controls follow the hierarchy of control and each has an owner, cost and date
The reply to the neighbour is respectful, factual and promises only what the plan supports
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Treat the case pack and the complaint letters as confidential; return all papers to the assessor
Do not use real firms' names or real people's details
Respect each other's views and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Environmental emergency procedure and tabletop exercise
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up scenario: a fuel and chemical store at a business in Jamaica, with a site plan and a list of equipment. Part A (1 hour): write a one-page emergency procedure for a fuel or chemical spill, covering roles, first steps, containing drains, equipment, contacts, reporting and clean-up. Part B (45 minutes): run a tabletop exercise. The assessor reads out a spill scenario in stages, such as a split drum during heavy rain at night, and the group talks through its response using the procedure and the site plan. Each member has a named role: incident controller (leads the response and makes decisions); spill response lead (explains how the spill will be contained and the drains protected); communications officer (decides who must be told, including the authority and neighbours, and drafts the first message); recorder (keeps a timed log of decisions); and reviewer (watches, notes gaps and leads the debrief). In a group of four, the recorder also leads the debrief. Part C (45 minutes): write an incident report and a short lessons-learned note with at least three improvements to the procedure, each with an owner and a date. Every member writes part of the report.
materials: Scenario cards, site plan and equipment list from the assessor
Procedure, incident report and action plan templates
Flipchart paper, markers and a clock or timer
Computer and printer, or paper and pens
photos: The site plan with drains, stores and spill kits marked
The tabletop exercise in progress (faces only if all agree)
The recorder's timed log of decisions
The incident report and the lessons-learned note
checklist: Took a named role and carried it out during the exercise
The procedure puts people's safety first and then contains the spill and protects drains
Reporting duties and contacts are identified in general terms
Decisions during the exercise follow the procedure and are logged with times
The incident report is factual and finds causes, not blame
Improvements are specific, with owners and dates
safety: This is a paper exercise only: no real chemicals or fuel are handled
Keep the debrief respectful: discuss actions, not personal faults
Use only made-up names and organisations
Share the writing fairly and take a short break between parts
